note: The answer correctly states the low-pH compensation problem the ~50 percent error figure and that temperature correction can be the largest error source but it omits the hydrogen-ion transport explanation the 25 °C equilibration check its ±5 μS/cm / ±3 percent pass bar and the comment-field recording requirement. Unmet: Explains the cause as the hydrogen ion having different transport properties and contributing a large share of the conductance at low pH; Describes the check of comparing the in-situ reading against the same water equilibrated to 25 C; Gives the pass bar for that check as within about 5 microsiemens per centimetre at or below 100 or about 3 percent above that; States that if an alternative low-pH compensation method is used the compensation factor has to be recorded in the comment field

The answer makes the qualifier/estimated-reporting atmospheric-exposure DO-and-temperature and inert-gas points but omits the in-situ-vs-recommended distinction and the suction-lift pump warning and commits no 'must not' violation. Unmet: ORP DO and temperature required in situ where possible while pH conductivity and turbidity only recommended; Warns a peristaltic/suction-lift pump must not be used for ORP or DO because negative pressure volatilises dissolved gases

The answer gives the reading schedule and thermal-equilibration timing but omits the in-situ/airtight-system requirement oxygen-impermeable tubing and purging ORP's slower/asymmetric response reporting Eh to the nearest 10 mV and logging the electrode system used. Unmet: measurement must be made in situ or through an airtight flowthrough system that eliminates aeration; tubing impermeable to oxygen fittings airtight atmospheric oxygen purged before measuring; ORP responds more slowly than pH and asymmetrically longer in one direction; calculated Eh reported to the nearest 10 mV; temperature electrode system used and pH at time of measurement must be recorded

The answer makes only the temperature-change point missing condensation the other bench biases the both-methods check and the equilibration/particle-association point though it avoids all the must-not violations. Unmet: Identifies condensation on the sample cell as a plausible source of bias when sample water is much colder than air; Names the other bench-measurement biases: cell orientation coloured water gas bubbles scratched or dirty sample cells; Explains the preference for in-situ or pumped dynamic measurement while requiring checks of both methods before deciding which reading is reliable; Notes that letting the sample equilibrate to ambient temperature reduces condensation but warming the sample can change particle associations

The answer declares the standard 4/7/10 buffers adequate at pH 3 (the prohibited claim) and misses four of the five must-contain points including the need for a pH 1.68/2 buffer the bracketing requirement the 10 C buffer-temperature rule and the 0.05 pH-unit check. Unmet: States the usual 4/7/10 buffer set is not sufficient for acidic water and a pH 1.68 (or 2) buffer is needed when acidic waters are measured; States the sample pH must fall inside the calibrated range so a 4/7/10 set does not bracket pH 3.2; States the calibration buffers must be within about 10 C of the sample temperature; States that a check of the buffer nearest the sample pH should be within about 0.05 pH unit of its value at that temperature or the system is recalibrated

The answer correctly states the subsample qualifier rule for turbidity temperature DO and Eh but it refuses the flow-cell sampling question and omits the storage limits and time-sensitivity guidance withholding facts the rubric expects. Unmet: States plainly that a discrete turbidity sample must not be collected from the discharge passing through the flow-through chamber holding the other sensors; Gives the storage limits if the sample cannot be read on site: clean amber bottle kept out of sunlight chilled at or below 4 C held no longer than 24 hours; Notes turbidity is time sensitive and should be measured on site preferably in situ

Unmet: Checking a temperature sensor means verifying accuracy across the range of use not adjusting it to a standard like pH/conductivity; A faulty or drifting thermistor in the conductivity cell produces wrong specific conductance values

Only the droplet-check/optical-caution point is made; the calibration-goal 0.1 C temperature mg/L computation ionic-strength-from-conductivity and both salinity-correction points are missing and no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Goal of one-point calibration is a 100% oxygen-saturated environment with DO sensor and its temperature sensor at the same temperature; Barometric pressure read at calibration time to nearest 1 mm Hg from a calibration-checked barometer; Temperature read to the nearest 0.1 C; Reported concentration computed from sensor signal with temperature and ionic strength; sensor does not measure mg/L directly; Ionic strength for salinity correction estimated from the conductivity measurement; Manual salinity correction preferred after calibration and measurement; distinguishes automatic conductivity-based compensation; Manual salinity correction at calibration forces recalibration for each change in field salinity
